data.name: Tricone Lab
data.detailed_description:
An abstract lateral-thinking puzzle game


In each level the aim is to build units of tricone within cell compartments. Change the cell structure for example by breaking open compartment walls. Once resources become available you can use catalysts to create compounds you need: each compound has a unique ability. As you progress, new resource, catalyst and compound types emerge within puzzles that increasingly challenge your lateral thinking.

Features

  • 100 unique puzzle levels.
  • A large variety of elements that all interact with each other.
  • Guided tutorial levels to introduce you to the gameplay and terminology.
  • Non-linear progression based on your mastery of particular elements.
  • Undo/Redo capabilities let you experiment with different approaches to each level.
  • Graphical level editor allows you to create your own puzzles.
  • Earn Steam Achievements as you master each set of puzzles.
  • Colour-blind mode.

About the developer

Partickhill Games Limited is a tiny indie gamedev operation based in Glasgow, Scotland.

Sound effects were contributed by Jack Menhorn and the music is by Iain Foxwell aka holobeams.

data.short_description: A unique abstract puzzle game with an emphasis on lateral thinking. Use catalysts to build compounds and manipulate cell structures. 100 puzzle levels and a level editor to create your own custom puzzle designs.

reviews.review:
Tricone Lab is a unique, "pure" puzzle game by a "microscopic indie developer". Pick it up if you are looking for an original puzzler to challenge your mind in new ways.

The "pure" refers to the focus on the puzzles. There is no story. There is a sort of biochemistry theme, but aside from the visual aesthetic, there's not any "actual" biochemistry going on here (so don't worry if that wasn't your favorite school subject). The visual "biochemistry" presentation is quite nice, unique, and carefully crafted (surely no small feat to program).

The gameplay is a sort of turn based resource management. The game is split into maps, which are split into several single screen levels. For each level, you must figure out how to get from the initial configuration to one satisfying the level requirement (producing some amount of tricone).

Although the puzzle mechanics are turn based in essence, the presentation is not static. The pieces you can interact with float freely inside of cell structures in real time. You interact with them by clicking and dragging - which does convey a sort of feeling of playing with microorganisms.

The mechanics are elegant, logical, well designed, and clearly introduced. There are three basic categories of pieces you can interact with: resources, catalysts, and compounds. Drag resources onto catalyst receptors to generate compounds. Compound pieces can be activated to manipulate the cells or other pieces.

I'm not aware of any other games quite like this, although it reminded me vaguely of working out chess puzzles. The mechanics are of course quite different, but there is similarity in satisfying a goal condition from a starting position using a set of pieces via a sequence of moves.

Like other resource management games, as well chess problems, the process is primarily deductive, but trial and error can sometimes be used as a crutch to a limited degree. The mechanics of tricone lab are quite clever, though, and require a higher degree of "lateral thinking" than most resource management games.

I am quite pleased at how tricone lab made me think in new ways ("lateral thinking"). This is very valuable to me in a game. I did find myself getting stuck on some levels a few times, but I moved on to other levels or took breaks, and eventually was able to get through all of the standard levels on my own, and felt quite good about that. Having the achievements to commemorate that is nice too ;)

The play time through the standard levels is roughly 10 hours, but will vary quite a bit up or down depending on how readily you pick up the mechanics.

The game includes a good level editor, and thus hopefully there will be quite a few more levels to play later on (there are already a few user maps that are quite decent).

There are a few rare glitches (and a common one), but none are gamebreaking - just a bit annoying sometimes. Hopefully these will be fixed eventually, but they hardly alter my positive opinion of the game at this point.

While technically still in Early Access, the game is complete and the difficulty is quite well tuned at this point. If interested and price not a factor, there is no reason to delay.

Disclosure: I received a free copy expressly without any obligations.
